Preparing to raise her first child, the author ponders how best to pass on the love and traditions of a big Greek family.

It’s New Year’s Day, and we’re in my grandparents’ backyard. Although the people are the same as at Christmas, today there is less pressure. Everyone is lying on blankets on the grass, in the sun, watching my cousin’s one-year-old, the first great-grandchild.

My partner, Damien, and I have driven from the beach, still covered in salt. I am in the same outfit I’ve been wearing for days, mostly because my clothes have stopped fitting me; the elastic band of my skirt is stretched over my growing stomach.

I’ve admitted that I’m pregnant only recently, even to myself – let alone my family. I treated the first months with so much caution, I almost feel as if I haven’t thought of it enough. When we found out we were having a boy I cried, mostly because I hadn’t prepared to have a boy. But then I cried because I was overwhelmed by the realisation that we had created an actual person, who would have a whole identity and a whole life, and I found the responsibility of that so profound.

Sitting next to me, my cousin tells me how hard it is going to be – the lost sleep, lost time – but here, now, she seems the happiest I’ve ever seen her. Her daughter has just started walking; we cheer as we watch her stagger over the grass.

When I think about building a life for someone, I’m surprised by how little resolve I have. What makes a good life? I want him to have this scene, mostly. Now that my grandparents are older, I will have to be the one to re-create it and all its components. Food is the most obvious. The olive oil-braised vegetables; the plates of feta. The smell of smoke off the spit is still hanging in the air, even though the leftovers have been cleared inside. Our meals are communal and happen often.

I collect Yiayia’s recipes, recording quantities and her methods as she cooks. Everything is done by eye, by feel, and so I have to stand watching over her shoulder, to see her use the lid of a bottle to measure oil, her hand to measure water into a dough, and then what it should feel like in her hand.

I assumed that the moment I became pregnant we would become mother and child, but now I realise it will be a lifelong process, a whole lifetime of inheritance.

Language is the harder element. We go to the Greek Centre in the city, one evening a week, to take classes with all the other diasporic Greeks trying to reconnect with their culture. Our teacher is enthusiastic, but the learning curve is steep. I am confronted by how little I know of the Greek language but also how little I know of how English is constructed.

“Will he want to learn Greek?” we say to each other. We’ll have to see what he likes. We hope he’ll like us.

“Do you think he’s happy?” Damien says, with his hand on my stomach, as our baby thrashes around.

We decide to give him a Greek name and choose Kosmas because, when we look it up, it symbolises cosmic order and harmony, which sounds beautiful and as if it carries real weight. Damien sends me pictures of Soviet mosaics of astronauts for weeks and I’m confused. When I eventually ask about them, he says, “Because he’s our cosmonaut.”

We read of saints Cosmas and Damian, twin physicians renowned for healing the sick and refusing payment for their services. They were called Anargyri, meaning The Silverless. They cured blindness, fever and paralysis.

We tell my mum his name and she says not much. Only that she hadn’t heard it often. But now she says “Hi Kos” and “Bye Kos”, instead of addressing me. She hands me a glass of water and when I say I don’t want it, she says, “It’s not for you.”

Damien and I decide to marry in a Greek church before “Kos” comes. Not exactly for religion, more for tradition: for the church, beauty and reverence. First, Damien has to be baptised. I sit in the front row during the service and cannot stop laughing – a mix of nerves and tenderness, watching him so nervous, earnest and sweet. He is bathed in an oversized plastic gardening bucket, wearing only his boxers. The priest draws a cross with oil on his forehead, behind his ears, on his knees, as if he were a baby. Damien is so tall, when the holy water is poured over his head, he keeps awkwardly trying to half-crouch to make it easier for the priest.

The church we choose for our wedding is the one in which I was baptised. Where my Yiayia still goes and where my Paupou used to go but now can’t be bothered. At our first appointment, we show one of the priests my baptism certificate and he says, “That’s my signature.” He is 92.

The priest who marries us is much younger. His phone ringtone is a choir of Orthodox monks chanting, which disrupts our every meeting. He keeps losing our marriage registry paperwork.

I stand with him at the doors of the church on our wedding day, looking over everyone before he leads Dad and me down the aisle. He turns to me and says, “This crowd is very Aussie, no?” I agree and he shrugs slightly. He begins to sing, starting the procession without waiting for the last of our friends to enter the church.

The ceremony is beautiful because of that mix of formality with the earnestness of everyone attending. Damien’s best man is shaking so much that when he goes to place the rings on our fingers, as is tradition, the priest has to tell him to take a deep breath and try again. In his closing speech, the priest instructs us to be dedicated to each other, even when it’s hard, and to now go and have children – at which Damien gestures to my protruding belly. The priest gasps.

Once we have been congratulated and kissed on both cheeks by every guest, and once we have signed our marriage certificate, the priest turns to me and asks, “Are you happy?” I know he means with the logistics of the day, but I am happy because it feels like a new beginning: a new attempt to dedicate ourselves to the culture, a new start at building a life.

In my grandparents’ backyard, I think of how that dedication is reflected in our time together now. My grandparents have always made this meal for the whole family on New Year’s Day, even though my cousins, sister and I refused to show up throughout our 20s. They have always been here waiting for us.

On Easter Sunday during the Melbourne Covid lockdowns, I used my one permitted hour of exercise to walk to my grandparents’, only to find that everyone in the family had done the same and they were all sitting on plastic chairs, socially distanced throughout the backyard. It’s this essence I want to give my son.

Lying in bed each night, in the moments before sleep, is when he seems most active. Even though the timing is consistent, and I should know to expect it, I find it confusing. Whose body is making that feeling? Or is it both of us together? I assumed that the moment I became pregnant we would become mother and child, but now I realise it will be a lifelong process, a whole lifetime of inheritance.

Ella Mittas is a chef and writer.
